questions.stem: Compared with the Sun, a high-mass star's main sequence life is…

options.explanation: Bigger stars burn brighter and faster.
More fuel, far faster burning — the lifetime shortens.
Mass changes the lifetime.
The comparison is a standard fact.

questions.stem: Past the main sequence, a high-mass star becomes a…

options.explanation: Not part of this sequence.
The supergiant stage precedes the supernova.
That is the solar-mass stage.
Solar-mass endpoint.

questions.stem: A higher-mass star fuses helium into…

options.explanation: Hydrogen is the fuel, not the product.
Fusion continues to heavier elements.

options.text: even heavier elements such as iron
options.explanation: Bigger stars build bigger nuclei.
Carbon is the lower-mass product.

questions.stem: A lower-mass star fuses helium into elements such as…

options.explanation: Iron belongs to the high-mass path.
Not a stellar fusion product here.
Helium is the fuel being fused.
Carbon is the quoted lower-mass product.

questions.stem: As a red supergiant forms, its surface…

options.text: expands and cools, turning the star red
options.explanation: Same physics as the red giant, at greater scale.
That is the collapse direction.
The star swells enormously.
Red signals the cooler surface.

questions.stem: State the stage a high-mass star enters after the main sequence.
State how a high-mass star's main sequence time compares with the Sun's.
questions.modelAnswer: Its main sequence stay runs shorter than the Sun's.

questions.stem: Explain why a high-mass star's fusion reaches heavier elements than the Sun's.
questions.modelAnswer: The larger star's core runs hotter, so its fusion builds helium into still heavier elements — iron among them — where a solar-mass star stops at carbon.

questions.stem: Two stars leave the main sequence: one Sun-like, one much larger. State each one's next stage.
questions.modelAnswer: The Sun-like star becomes a red giant; the much larger star becomes a red supergiant.

questions.stem: A supernova happens when…

options.text: the core slowly shrinks for a billion years
options.explanation: The collapse is sudden.

options.text: fusion inside the red supergiant can no longer continue and the core collapses suddenly
options.explanation: Core collapse sets off the gigantic explosion.
Hydrogen fusion is the stable phase.
Planets are irrelevant here.

questions.stem: What forms at the centre of a supernova?

options.explanation: A dense body forms, not emptiness.
The giant stage is already past.

options.text: a dense body called a neutron star
options.explanation: The collapsed core becomes the neutron star.
No new main sequence star forms there.

questions.stem: The supernova's outer remnants become…

options.explanation: White dwarfs form in solar-mass deaths.
The remnants are clouds of dust and gas.
Only the most massive cores go further.

options.text: new clouds of dust and gas — nebulae
options.explanation: Ejected remnants seed new nebulae.

questions.stem: Where are the heaviest elements formed?

options.text: during a supernova, then ejected into space
options.explanation: The explosion forges and scatters the heaviest elements.

options.text: inside a nebula before the star forms
options.explanation: Nebulae are clouds, not forges.
White dwarfs do not forge heavy elements.
Planetary cores do not fuse elements.

questions.stem: The ejected supernova remnants may later…

options.text: orbit the neutron star forever unchanged
options.explanation: They are ejected into space, not locked in orbit.
The nebulae of ejected remnants can seed new systems.

options.text: collapse into planets directly without any cloud
options.explanation: The cloud stage comes first.
They persist as nebulae and new systems.

questions.stem: State what a supernova is.
questions.modelAnswer: A gigantic explosion that follows the sudden collapse of the core when fusion can no longer continue.

questions.stem: Name the dense body formed at the centre of a supernova.
questions.modelAnswer: A neutron star forms at the centre.

questions.stem: Explain why a supernova seeds new planetary systems.
questions.modelAnswer: The explosion ejects the star's outer remnants into space as clouds of dust and gas — nebulae — and those nebulae may later collapse into new planetary systems.

questions.stem: An astronomer finds unusually heavy elements in a young nebula. State the likely origin.
questions.modelAnswer: The heaviest elements are formed during supernovae and ejected into space, so a supernova likely forged and scattered them.

questions.stem: For the most massive stars, the neutron star at the supernova's centre…

options.explanation: The core stays dense.
Collapse continues in the most massive cases.

options.text: continues collapsing under gravity into a black hole
options.explanation: Only the most massive cores collapse that far.

options.text: turns back into a red supergiant
options.explanation: Stages do not reverse.

questions.stem: A black hole is…

options.text: a giant cloud of glowing gas
options.explanation: That describes a nebula.

options.text: a hole in the Earth's surface
options.explanation: Nothing terrestrial here.

options.text: a star that emits mainly blue light
options.explanation: Black holes emit nothing that escapes.

options.text: an extremely dense object with gravity so strong not even light escapes
options.explanation: Both density and the light-trapping gravity are required.

questions.stem: What force drives the final collapse to a black hole?

options.explanation: Gravity crushes the core past the neutron star stage.
Magnetism is not the collapsing agent.
Fusion has already failed.
Repulsion pushes apart; collapse needs attraction.

questions.stem: Which is true of light near a black hole?

options.explanation: Escape is the issue, not speed-up.

options.text: not even light can escape its gravity
options.explanation: Light-trapping is the black hole's signature.

options.text: light orbits it as a satellite
options.explanation: The of-record statement is that light cannot escape.
Gravity overwhelms light there.

questions.stem: The endpoint of the most massive stars is…

options.explanation: A mid-life stage, not an endpoint.
Nebulae form from remnants, not the core's fate.
Supergiant → supernova → neutron star, then black hole for the largest.
That endpoint belongs to solar-mass stars.

questions.stem: Name the two possible endpoints left after a supernova.
questions.modelAnswer: A neutron star, or — for the most massive stars — a black hole.

questions.stem: Define a black hole.
questions.modelAnswer: An object of extreme density whose gravitational pull traps even light: nothing, light included, can escape it.

questions.stem: Explain why the most massive stars end differently from solar-mass stars.
questions.modelAnswer: Their collapsed cores are so massive that gravity keeps crushing the neutron star further, forming a black hole, whereas a solar-mass star simply settles into a white dwarf and cools.

questions.stem: A dying star is ten times the Sun's mass. Predict its path after the main sequence.
questions.modelAnswer: Red supergiant → supernova → neutron star, and given the large mass, likely onward to a black hole.
